title: This Ancient Volcano Froze the Andes in Their Baby Stage — 22 Million Years Ago
summary: Imagine a volcano so powerful it buried an entire mountain range under a thick blanket of ash. That's exactly what happened in northern Chile 22 million years ago. The eruption came from the Lauca Caldera and sent a pyroclastic flow — a deadly mix of rock, gas, and ash — sweeping across the landscape like a boiling tsunami. This is the same phenomenon that buried Pompeii in A.D. 79, but on a much larger scale. The flow left behind a rock called ignimbrite, which preserved the landscape beneath it. Now, a new study published in Science Advances has peered under that volcanic blanket. Researchers found that the Andes were not towering peaks back then. They were rolling foothills. The mountains were rising at a rate of no more than 0.16 miles (0.26 kilometers) per million years — an incredibly slow process. "Pompeii shows how volcanic eruptions can freeze a moment in human history," said Byron Adams, a geomorphologist at University College London. "This study shows that much larger eruptions can also freeze moments in Earth history, burying whole landscapes beneath volcanic deposits and preserving clues to how mountains were being built before the eruption." The findings support the idea that the Andes grew slowly and steadily over 40 to 50 million years, rather than popping up recently. The same method could be used to study other mountain ranges worldwide. So the next time you see a mountain, remember: it might have taken millions of years to grow — and a volcano might have saved its baby picture.
why_it_matters: This story shows how scientists can read millions of years of Earth's history from a single layer of rock, and understanding how mountains grow slowly helps explain the forces that shape continents, trigger earthquakes, and change landscapes over time.

background_read: Pompeii was a Roman city in Italy that was buried when Mount Vesuvius erupted in A.D. 79. The ash fell so fast that buildings, food, and even the shapes of people were preserved for archaeologists to find many centuries later.

The Andes are the long mountain chain running down the western side of South America. They are still growing because the Nazca Plate — a slab of ocean floor — slides slowly underneath the South American continent and pushes the land upward.

Science Advances is a peer-reviewed journal published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the same organization behind the journal Science. 'Peer-reviewed' means other scientists check the work before it is published.
University College London is a large research university in London, England, where Byron Adams studies how landscapes are shaped and changed.

Other great ranges grew in the same slow way: the Himalayas were built when the Indian subcontinent drifted into Asia tens of millions of years ago, which is why geologists think mountain ranges usually take tens of millions of years to form.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a rare window into the past
perspectives.description: The ash layer acted like a lid, keeping the ancient landscape intact so researchers could measure how fast the Andes were rising. That gives geologists a new tool for studying mountain belts around the world.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — one site may not tell the whole story
perspectives.description: A single eruption's deposit shows conditions in one place at one moment. The slow-growth numbers from northern Chile may not apply to every part of the Andes, or to ranges built by different kinds of plate collisions.

Volcanic eruptions, floods, and mudslides have long preserved snapshots of the past, from Pompeii to fossil beds. Earth scientists increasingly treat these layers as time capsules that record a single dramatic moment in deep time.

The team suggests the same technique could be applied to other mountain ranges. If it works broadly, it could sharpen models of plate tectonics and help predict how today's growing ranges might change in the future.
